title: Snacking is becoming a flexible food, social, and emotional infrastructure balancing convenience, health, indulgence, and connection
source_unit: Mondelēz International, 2026 State of Snacking, developed with Mintel and Black Swan Data
geography: Selected global markets across North America, Latin America, Europe, Asia, and Australia; market-specific survey bases vary

denominator.unit: selected-market consumer survey frame; market-specific internet-user and adult samples reported in the source

daily_snacking.unit: in 10 consumers in selected global markets snack at least once a day

social_necessity.unit: in 3 consumers in selected markets say snacks are necessary when socializing with friends or family

social_discovery.unit: percent of Indian adults agreeing it is fun to try new snacks with friends to see their reactions

social_media_inspiration.unit: share of consumers in selected markets citing social media as a source of snacking inspiration

observations.method: Mintel consumer research across market-specific samples, supplemented by Black Swan Data analysis of social and online posts; denominators and field dates vary by market.
observations.uncertainty: The selected-market aggregate is not a globally representative estimate; social-media conversation is not equivalent to population behavior, and the corporate sponsor frames the category through commercial trend analysis.
observations.subgroup: Snack consumers across selected markets, with explicit India and market-specific age comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Snacking can support social connection and rituals while also displacing shared meals or reflecting time scarcity, household fragmentation, and marketing exposure.

observations.period: 2025; snacks as meal replacement and time-saving consumption

denominator.unit: selected-market consumer samples; examples include Australia, Canada, and aggregate selected markets

meal_replacement.unit: approximately percent of consumers in selected markets occasionally replacing meals with snacks

australia_weekly_substitution.unit: percent of Australian snack consumers agreeing they snack instead of a proper meal at least once a week

canada_weekly_substitution.unit: percent of Canadian cooks swapping snacks for meals weekly

stated_benefits.value: saving cooking stress, balancing healthy and unhealthy choices, and better perceived value than meals

observations.method: Mintel market-specific consumer surveys of snack consumers and people with cooking responsibility; examples are not pooled into one common denominator.
observations.uncertainty: Meal replacement may reflect convenience, affordability, work schedules, household routines, or preference; the report does not establish nutritional adequacy, food insecurity, or health effects.
observations.subgroup: Younger consumers, household cooks, workers, students, solo households, and people managing time or food budgets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Flexible eating can reduce preparation burden and support autonomy, but it may also shift food labor and health risks into households while increasing reliance on packaged products.

denominator.unit: selected global-market consumer samples; country bases vary

healthier_choice.unit: approximately percent of snack consumers looking for healthier snacks at least some of the time

satiety_priority.unit: approximately percent of snacking occasions where satiety is emerging as a priority

texture_signal.unit: percent of Thai adults agreeing snack crunch and crackle creates an enjoyable sensory experience

savoring.unit: percent of UK adults trying to savor the experience when eating or drinking

observations.method: Mintel survey data combined with qualitative and social-listening trend synthesis; market-specific questions and samples are retained as reported.
observations.uncertainty: Health-seeking, satiety, and sensory preferences do not measure nutritional quality, consumption volume, or long-term health outcomes; commercial definitions of better-for-you vary.
observations.subgroup: Snack consumers seeking different combinations of health, protein/fiber, portion control, texture, taste, and sensory novelty.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same occasion can combine health intentions with indulgence; consumer demand for better-for-you options may produce reformulation, portioning, or premiumization rather than lower total consumption.

observations.period: 2025-2026; emotional and cultural meaning of snacks

denominator.unit: global consumer-trend synthesis across selected markets

productive_tensions.value: health and indulgence; nostalgia and novelty; solo convenience and social connection

comfort_and_reward.value: snacks are described as sources of comfort, reward, and small moments of indulgence

nostalgia_route.value: nostalgia can be expressed through flavors, packaging, and formats

category_expansion.value: snacks are framed as daily rituals, social tools, meal substitutes, and sensory experiences rather than only between-meal bites

observations.method: Publisher synthesis of Mintel consumer research and Black Swan Data social/online-post analysis, supplemented by future-trend partner perspectives.
observations.uncertainty: Cultural meanings are interpreted through a branded category lens and should not be generalized to all food practices, cuisines, or communities.
observations.subgroup: Consumers using food for routine, reward, identity, nostalgia, social connection, convenience, and sensory exploration.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same trends can indicate creative adaptation and connection or the commercialization of emotional needs, time scarcity, and social fragmentation.

related_sources.claim: FAO food-security evidence provides a complementary affordability, nutrition, and food-system lens beyond commercial snacking behavior.
IKEA Life at Home 2026 provides complementary household time, health, comfort, and consumer-pressure context.
OECD-FAO Agricultural Outlook provides complementary production, price, diet, and food-system context.

boundary: This record adds a food-culture and consumer route linking snacking to social connection, meal substitution, time pressure, health intentions, sensory novelty, nostalgia, and emotional reward. It uses a branded commercial trend study with market-specific surveys and social listening, not nationally pooled dietary surveillance, nutritional assessment, causal health evidence, food-insecurity measurement, or a globally representative estimate.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Mondelēz State of Snacking 2026 page and linked Mintel/Mondelēz PDF were reviewed for executive findings, market-specific denominators, survey methodology, social-listening method, and interpretation boundaries.
